issues.description: In Experiment 1, 17 out of 40 participants (42.5%) were excluded from analysis due to having too few high confidence critical trials (≤10 trials in one or more cells). This is an extremely high exclusion rate that raises serious concerns about the generalizability of the findings and suggests the task design may not reliably elicit high-confidence responses. The remaining 23 participants may represent a biased subsample (e.g., those with higher overall confidence or different response strategies). Similarly, in Experiment 2, 92 out of 290 participants (31.7%) were excluded. These exclusion rates are not adequately discussed in terms of their implications for the validity of the findings.
issues.quote: Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence critical trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) were excluded from the analysis resulted in an inclusion of 23 participants (17 participants were excluded)

issues.description: The threshold for excluding participants (≤10 high confidence trials per cell) appears arbitrary and is not justified. No pre-registration is mentioned for any of the four experiments, and the choice of this cutoff represents a researcher degree of freedom that could substantially affect results. Different thresholds (e.g., 5 or 15 trials) could yield different included samples and potentially different results. The authors do not report sensitivity analyses examining how results change under different exclusion thresholds.
issues.quote: Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence critical trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less) were excluded from the analysis

issues.subcategory: Confound between delay and interference conditions
issues.description: In Experiment 1, the three memory conditions differ in multiple ways simultaneously. The 'Short with Interference' condition differs from the 'Short' condition in both the presence of interference AND the temporal relationship between the cue and the irrelevant display. The 'Long' condition differs from the 'Short' condition in delay duration but also in the timing of the irrelevant second display relative to the cue. This makes it impossible to cleanly attribute differences between conditions to any single factor (time, interference, or their interaction).
issues.quote: In two conditions the memory probe appeared 0.75 seconds after offset of the memory display, in the third memory condition, the probe appeared 3 seconds after offset of the memory display. If the probe appeared 0.75 seconds after memory display offset, it either appeared together with the irrelevant second display (the Short-with-interference condition), or it appeared in isolation (the Short condition).

issues.subcategory: Confidence scale as proxy for memory illusions
issues.description: The entire theoretical framework rests on the assumption that high-confidence errors reflect genuine illusory memories (i.e., the participant has a vivid but false memory trace) rather than other processes. However, a 4-point confidence scale (1=guess to 4=certain) is a coarse measure. The authors dichotomize responses into 'high confidence' (presumably ratings of 3-4, though this is never explicitly stated) and 'low confidence,' but the exact cutoff for 'high confidence' is never specified. Moreover, high confidence in an error could reflect metacognitive failure rather than a genuine illusory memory experience.
issues.quote: Subsequently she indicated confidence in her judgment (1 = guess, 4 = certainty).

issues.description: The authors repeatedly analyze 'high confidence trials' but never explicitly define which confidence ratings (on the 1-4 scale) constitute 'high confidence.' It is unclear whether this means only rating 4, ratings 3-4, or some other threshold. This is critical because the entire analysis and all conclusions depend on this distinction.
issues.quote: Exclusion of participants with too few high confidence trials in one or more cells of the design (10 trials or less)

issues.description: Table 4 (Follow-up ANOVA for other, non-illusory error-rates in Experiment 2) shows BFincl = 0.064 for Memory Delay and BFincl = 39110.895 for Target Type. However, the text states 'Non-illusory error rates increased from the short to the long delay (BFincl = 190 for Memory Delay) but this increase was the same for pseudo- and real letter targets.' The BFincl of 190 reported in the text does not match the BFincl of 0.064 shown in Table 4 for Memory Delay. Additionally, the text says 'the other (non-illusory) error rate was not influenced by target-type (11% for real-letter and pseudo-letter targets)' but Table 4 shows BFincl = 39110.895 for Target Type, suggesting a very strong effect of target type on non-illusory errors.
issues.quote: Non-illusory error rates increased from the short to the long delay (BFincl = 190 for Memory Delay) but this increase was the same for pseudo- and real letter targets (2% increase, from 10 to 12%, in both real and pseudo-letter targets).

issues.description: In Table 4, the BFincl for Memory Delay is 0.064, which constitutes substantial evidence AGAINST including Memory Delay in the model (by the authors' own interpretation guidelines). Yet the text claims 'BFincl = 190 for Memory Delay' and interprets this as evidence that non-illusory error rates increased with longer delays. Either the table or the text contains an error, and this discrepancy fundamentally affects the interpretation of whether non-illusory errors also increase with delay.
issues.quote: For other, non-illusory errors only Memory Delay was a relevant factor (BFm = 42...Non-illusory error rates increased from the short to the long delay (BFincl = 190 for Memory Delay)

issues.description: In Experiment 1, the response display design was asymmetric: when the target was a pseudo-letter, its real counterpart appeared as a response option on only 50% of critical trials, while when the target was a real letter, its pseudo counterpart appeared on only ~16% of trials. This means the base rates for being able to make illusory errors differed between conditions. Although the authors acknowledge this and address it in Experiment 2, the Experiment 1 results are still interpreted as supporting the hypotheses without adequately accounting for this confound.
issues.quote: If the target was a pseudo-letter, then it appeared as a response option randomly on half of those trials while on the other half of pseudo-letter trials only the real counterpart was one of the response options. If the target was a real letter, then it appeared as a response option on a randomly selected 83% of the trials, while its mirror reversed (pseudo-letter) version appeared as a response option on the other 16% of the trials.

issues.subcategory: Decay vs. interference confound for causal claims
issues.description: The authors claim that the increase in illusory errors over time demonstrates that the illusions are memory-based rather than perception-based. However, the longer delay conditions also involve more opportunity for internal rehearsal, reconsolidation, and other cognitive processes. The increase could reflect retrieval-stage reconstruction rather than changes to the stored memory trace itself. The authors' causal claim that 'correctly encoded percepts of a pseudo-letter are being converted to illusory memories of a real letter' during storage is one interpretation, but retrieval-based reconstruction is equally plausible and not ruled out.
issues.quote: Over time illusions become more prevalent, indicating that correctly encoded percepts of a pseudo-letter are being converted to illusory memories of a real letter.

issues.description: To distinguish perceptual from memory illusions, the authors rely on the increase of errors over time. However, a more direct test would include a condition where participants report while the stimulus is still visible (a perceptual baseline). Without this, the 'short delay' condition (500-750ms after offset) already involves memory processes, so the baseline level of errors at the shortest delay could already include substantial memory-based illusions, making the time-based argument less compelling.
issues.quote: if you only test at one single moment after disappearance of the stimuli, then any illusion can either be perceptual...or memory-based

issues.description: All four experiments use only mirrored letters as stimuli. While the authors acknowledge this limitation briefly in the discussion (referencing Chalk et al.), they make broad claims about 'short-term memory illusions' and 'world knowledge shaping memory' that go well beyond what letter-mirror stimuli can demonstrate. Letters are a very specific, highly overlearned category, and the findings may not generalize to other types of visual stimuli or other forms of world knowledge.
issues.quote: it suggests that internal priors play a crucial role not just during perception, but also in memory. Thus, it seems that short-term memory is not always an accurate representation of what was just perceived.

issues.subcategory: Online data collection without adequate controls
issues.description: Experiment 4 was conducted online via Zoom with participants using their own laptops. This introduces substantial variability in display conditions (screen size, resolution, refresh rate, viewing distance, ambient lighting) that could affect the perception and memory of letter stimuli. The authors do not discuss how these factors might influence results or whether any quality checks were implemented beyond the practice block supervision.
issues.quote: the data was collected in an online experiment, using Neurotask scripting. Participants that signed up to take part in the experiment were invited to join a Zoom meeting at a preset time. Here, each participant was placed in a Zoom break-out room, and given the link to the Neurotask experiment, which they then started on their own laptop.

issues.description: Experiments 3 and 4 used a sequential Bayesian stopping rule, checking 'every other day of testing' and stopping when BF crossed 10 for a specific t-test. However, the specific t-test used as the stopping criterion (comparison between the effect of Error-Type for Real and Pseudo-letter targets) is one of the key hypothesis tests. This means data collection was stopped precisely when the key result was significant, which can inflate false positive rates even with Bayesian methods if the stopping rule is not properly accounted for. Additionally, the exact number of interim analyses conducted is not reported.
issues.quote: Every other day of testing, the sequential analysis was run, and once the outcome crossed a BF of 10, testing would stop.

issues.description: The authors never report overall accuracy rates (proportion correct) for any experiment. This makes it difficult to evaluate the general difficulty of the task and whether participants were performing adequately. Knowing the overall correct response rate would help contextualize the error rates and assess whether the task was appropriately calibrated.

issues.subcategory: Missing effect sizes and descriptive statistics
issues.description: Throughout all four experiments, the authors report only Bayes Factors and percentage error rates. No traditional effect sizes (Cohen's d, eta-squared), standard deviations, or standard errors for the key comparisons are reported. While Bayesian analysis is a valid approach, the absence of effect sizes makes it difficult to evaluate the practical significance of the findings and to compare across experiments.

In Experiment 4, the text refers to 'Figure 5 shows the error rates for high confidence trials' but Figure 5 is already used for Experiment 3. The actual figure for Experiment 4 appears to be Figure 6 based on the figure caption provided later. This suggests a numbering error in the manuscript.
issues.quote: Figure 5 shows the error rates for high confidence trials. A Bayesian repeated measures ANOVA model comparison showed that the model with main effects for Error Type, Target Type, Memory Delay...

issues.subcategory: Response bias not fully ruled out
issues.description: The authors argue against response bias by noting that the asymmetry between pseudo-to-real and real-to-pseudo errors is stronger for high-confidence than low-confidence trials. However, this argument assumes that response bias should be stronger for low-confidence trials, which is not necessarily true. A response bias could interact with confidence in complex ways—for instance, participants might be more confident precisely because they selected the familiar (real letter) option, creating a circular relationship between confidence and the bias itself.
issues.quote: if the illusory reports are actually not illusions, but due to response bias, then the pattern of responses that can be attributed to a response bias...should be even stronger for the low-confidence responses

issues.description: The authors dismiss Fuzzy Trace Theory (FTT) by arguing that FTT predicts high similarity between target and lure should inhibit false memories, which contradicts their data. However, this may be a misapplication of FTT. FTT's similarity-inhibition prediction applies primarily to recognition paradigms (DRM-type tasks) where similar items help discriminate targets from lures at the verbatim level. In the current forced-choice paradigm, the mechanism is quite different—participants must select from options, not judge old/new. The authors' argument against FTT may therefore be based on an inappropriate application of FTT predictions to their specific paradigm.
issues.quote: FTT predicts that high similarity between a target and its mirrored counterpart should inhibit false memories. This is not consistent with the current data: The mirrored counterpart (the real letter) and the target (the pseudo-letter) are extremely similar, yet false memories are abundant.

issues.description: Experiment 1 included a training phase with a 75% accuracy exclusion criterion, while Experiments 2-4 did not include this training. This means the participant pools across experiments differ systematically in their demonstrated visual memory proficiency. The authors justify dropping the training to reduce time on task, but this creates a confound when comparing results across experiments.
issues.quote: Since only 10% of participants were excluded from participating in the main experiment based on the training scores, the training procedure was not part of Experiments 2, 3 and 4 in order to not make the overall time on task too long.

issues.description: The authors state that symmetrical letters were excluded but do not provide the complete list of letters that were used in the experiments. Since the visual similarity between a letter and its mirror varies considerably across different letters (e.g., 'b' vs 'd' is more confusable than 'F' vs reversed-F), knowing which specific letters were used is important for evaluating and replicating the study.
issues.quote: the symmetrical letters A,H,I,M,O,T,U,V,W,X,Y were excluded from the memory and response displays

issues.description: The authors state their BF interpretation guidelines with BF > 10 as 'strong evidence,' but throughout the paper they report BFs > 1000 simply as '>1000' without distinguishing between, say, BF = 1,001 and BF = 10^14. More importantly, for the critical Memory Delay × Error Type interaction in Experiment 1, the BFincl is only 4.21, which by their own criteria constitutes only 'substantial' evidence. Yet this interaction is central to Hypothesis 2 and is treated as strong support for the claim that illusions are memory-based rather than perceptual.
issues.quote: The interaction between Error Type and Memory Delay, (BFincl = 4.21) shows support for hypothesis 2

issues.description: The authors acknowledge but do not fully address the possibility that pseudo-letters simply have weaker memory traces that decay faster, leading to more errors of all types. While they argue that illusory errors increase more than other errors, the differential increase could be explained by the fact that when memory for a pseudo-letter degrades, the most available replacement in the response display is the visually similar real letter (which also happens to be the familiar one). This does not require invoking 'world knowledge reshaping memory traces' but simply differential accessibility of response options when memory is weak.
issues.quote: our findings clearly show that pseudo-letter targets do not simply lead to weaker memory traces. If that were the case, participants remembering a pseudo-letter target...should be selecting all items in the probe display with equal probability

issues.description: The forced-choice response format (selecting from 6 options) means that the presence of the real letter counterpart in the response display could cue or trigger the illusion at the point of retrieval/response, rather than the illusion existing in the memory trace itself. When a participant with a degraded memory trace sees the familiar real letter in the response options, this could trigger a false sense of recognition. This retrieval-cue explanation is distinct from the authors' claim that the memory trace itself has been transformed.
issues.quote: The response screen consisted of 6 letters: the target letter (with the same orientation as in the memory display, or mirror reversed), two other randomly selected letters from the memory display, and 3 letters that did not appear in the memory display.

issues.description: Participants received trial-by-trial feedback in all experiments. This feedback could itself influence expectations and response strategies over the course of the experiment. For instance, receiving 'incorrect' feedback when selecting a pseudo-letter (because the target was actually the real letter) could reinforce a bias toward selecting real letters. The authors do not analyze whether illusory memory rates changed over the course of the experiment (e.g., first half vs. second half), which would help assess whether feedback-driven learning contributed to the effects.
issues.quote: They were instructed to select "none of these" if the target letter was not a response option. After selecting the target letter, participants indicated their confidence by clicking on one of four boxes

issues.description: The abstract states illusions occur 'within 1 or 2 seconds' but the actual short delay conditions are 0.75s (Experiment 1) or 0.5s (Experiments 2-4) after memory display offset, and the long delay is 3 seconds. The General Discussion mentions '500 ms' and '3 seconds.' The abstract's '1 or 2 seconds' does not accurately describe any of the actual delay conditions used.
issues.quote: participants go from reliably reporting what was there (perceptual inference accurately reflecting the bottom-up input), to erroneously but with high confidence reporting what they expected to be there (memory report strongly influenced by top-down expectations)

issues.description: Experiments 2, 3, and 4 all used first-year psychology students participating for course credit. This is a very homogeneous sample (predominantly young, educated, likely familiar with psychological experiments). The authors make broad claims about how 'memory is shaped by what we expected to see' without acknowledging these sample limitations. Additionally, all participants were presumably literate in the Latin alphabet; the findings may not generalize to individuals with different writing systems.
issues.quote: The participants participated for student credits as part of a course within the first-year Psychology curriculum.

issues.subcategory: Selective analysis of high-confidence trials only
issues.description: The primary analyses focus exclusively on high-confidence trials, which is justified theoretically but also represents a substantial researcher degree of freedom. The authors do briefly mention low-confidence results in the Experiment 1 discussion to argue against response bias, but a complete analysis of all confidence levels (or a continuous analysis using confidence as a predictor) would provide a more comprehensive picture and reduce concerns about selective reporting.
issues.quote: isolating high confidence responses is necessary to identify those responses that reflect a participant having an actual, albeit false, memory of perceiving something that was not there

issues.description: The manuscript repeatedly references 'Appendix 1' for full model comparisons, but this appendix is not included in the manuscript. Without these full model comparisons, it is impossible to verify the reported Bayes Factors or assess whether alternative models provide competitive fits.
issues.quote: see Appendix 1 for full model comparison

issues.description: In Experiment 2, the color of the fixation cross indicated the probability of a pseudo-letter target (red = 25% pseudo, blue = 60% pseudo). However, participants were never explicitly told about this contingency, and the post-experiment questionnaire confirmed no participant noticed it. The null effect of cue color is therefore unsurprising—the manipulation may simply have been too subtle to generate any expectations. The authors interpret this as evidence that 'expectations need substantial time to develop,' but it could simply mean the manipulation failed to induce any expectations at all.
issues.quote: The relationship between the colour of the cue and the nature of the target was not mentioned in any of the responses. This experiment contained two memory delay conditions (short and long), two target types (real and pseudo) and two fixation color conditions (red and blue).

issues.description: The authors argue that the increase in illusions over time rules out perceptual encoding errors. However, they also acknowledge that some illusions are present even at the shortest delay (e.g., 29% in Experiment 1 short condition for pseudo-letter targets). This substantial baseline rate of illusions at the earliest time point is consistent with a large perceptual encoding component, with only the incremental increase attributable to memory processes. The authors' framing minimizes the potential perceptual contribution.
issues.quote: when probed 0.75 seconds after the memory display has disappeared, people correctly report what they saw in 70% of high confidence trials, thus showing that initial perceptual encoding was relatively intact
